rubric.why: This defines the proportion of solute by mass in a given volume of solution.
rubric.description: Defines m/v percentage as the mass of solute in 100 cm³ (or 100 mL) of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the mass of solute present in 100 cm³ or 100 mL of solution; accept equivalent wording or the formula.

rubric.why: The formula expresses the definition as a percentage.
rubric.description: Gives the formula for m/v percentage.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the formula: (mass of solute in g ÷ volume of solution in cm³) × 100.

modelAnswer: Mass/volume percentage is the mass of solute, in grams, dissolved in 100 cm³ of solution.
m/v percentage = (mass of solute in g ÷ volume of solution in cm³) × 100

items.followUp: What are strong electrolytes? Give one example.

rubric.why: Partial ionization or dissociation is the defining feature of a weak electrolyte.
rubric.description: States that weak electrolytes ionize or dissociate only partially in solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that only some of the dissolved electrolyte forms ions.

rubric.why: A suitable example completes the response.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of a weak electrolyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid example, such as acetic acid.

modelAnswer: Weak electrolytes are substances that ionize only partially into ions in aqueous solution.
Acetic acid (CH₃COOH) is an example.

items.followUp: State four postulates of Dalton’s atomic theory.

rubric.why: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy definite permitted orbits around the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed orbits or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying definite, fixed orbits or energy levels.

rubric.why: Electrons in permitted stationary orbits do not continuously lose energy.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not emit or absorb energy while in a permitted stationary orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this stationary-orbit property.

rubric.why: The permitted orbits are restricted by the quantization of electron angular momentum.
rubric.description: States that only certain orbits are allowed, with quantized angular momentum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that angular momentum is quantized, or giving mvr = nh/2π.

rubric.why: The energy of the permitted shells increases with distance from the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that electron orbits farther from the nucleus have greater energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship between orbit distance and energy.

rubric.why: Energy is exchanged when an electron moves between permitted orbits.
rubric.description: Explains that an electron absorbs or emits a definite amount of energy during a transition between orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing energy absorption or emission during a transition; the energy change may be stated as ΔE = hν.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed circular orbits called energy levels or shells.
An electron in a permitted orbit does not radiate or absorb energy; its energy remains constant.
Only certain orbits are allowed, and the electron’s angular momentum is quantized: mvr = nh/2π.
The energy of an orbit increases as its distance from the nucleus increases.
An electron absorbs or emits a definite amount of energy when it jumps between orbits; ΔE = hν.

items.followUp: Write four factors that affect the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: Temperature affects the kinetic energy and movement of particles.
rubric.description: Identifies temperature as a factor affecting diffusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for temperature.

rubric.why: A steeper concentration difference increases the net movement of particles.
rubric.description: Identifies concentration difference or concentration gradient as a factor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for concentration or concentration gradient.

rubric.why: Smaller or lighter particles generally diffuse more rapidly.
rubric.description: Identifies particle size or mass as a factor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for particle size or molecular mass.

rubric.why: The medium through which particles diffuse affects their rate of movement.
rubric.description: Identifies the nature, state, or density of the medium as a factor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the medium (for example, its nature, state, or density).

modelAnswer: Temperature: diffusion is faster at higher temperatures.
Concentration gradient: a larger concentration difference increases the rate of diffusion.
Particle size or mass: smaller and lighter particles diffuse faster.
Nature or density of the medium: diffusion is faster through a less dense medium.

items.followUp: Write four physical properties of metals.

rubric.why: Lack of lustre is a common physical property of non-metals.
rubric.description: States that non-metals are generally dull or non-lustrous.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for dullness or lack of lustre.

rubric.why: Solid non-metals are generally brittle rather than malleable or ductile.
rubric.description: States that solid non-metals are brittle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for brittleness.

rubric.why: Non-metals generally conduct heat and electricity poorly.
rubric.description: States that non-metals are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for poor conductivity.

rubric.why: These are other commonly taught physical properties of non-metals.
rubric.description: Gives one further correct physical property of non-metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct property such as low melting/boiling points, low density, or being non-sonorous.

modelAnswer: Non-metals are generally dull and non-lustrous.
Solid non-metals are brittle.
They are generally poor conductors of heat and electricity.
They generally have low melting and boiling points.

items.followUp: What is a radical? Explain how a free radical is formed.

rubric.why: An unpaired electron is the key feature of a free radical.
rubric.description: Defines a free radical as an atom or group of atoms containing an unpaired electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a free radical has at least one unpaired electron.

rubric.why: Homolytic bond breaking produces radicals by sharing the bonding electrons equally.
rubric.description: Explains that free radicals form when a covalent bond breaks homolytically.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that each bonded atom takes one electron when the covalent bond splits; heat or ultraviolet light may initiate the process.

modelAnswer: A free radical is an atom or group of atoms containing an unpaired electron.
It is generated when a covalent bond breaks homolytically, so each bonded atom takes one electron from the bond.

items.followUp: Calculate the formula mass of CaCO₃. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)

rubric.why: The formula contains two potassium atoms, one sulfur atom, and four oxygen atoms.
rubric.description: Sets up the formula-mass calculation using the correct atomic masses and subscripts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 2(39) + 32 + 4(16), or an equivalent correct setup.

rubric.why: The correctly evaluated total is 174 atomic mass units.
rubric.description: Calculates and states the formula mass with an appropriate unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 174 amu (or 174 u).

modelAnswer: Formula mass of K₂SO₄ = 2(K) + 1(S) + 4(O).
Formula mass = 2(39) + 32 + 4(16) amu.
Formula mass = 78 + 32 + 64 amu = 174 amu.

items.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of chlorine (atomic number 17) in shells and subshells.

rubric.why: The first two shells contain two and eight electrons, respectively.
rubric.description: Correctly gives the electron distribution in the first and second shells, or the corresponding subshells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 2, 8 in shell notation or 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ in subshell notation.

rubric.why: Argon’s third shell contains eight electrons, completing its distribution of 18 electrons.
rubric.description: Correctly gives the third-shell distribution and completes the configuration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the complete shell configuration 2, 8, 8 or the complete subshell configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶.

modelAnswer: Argon has 18 electrons.
Shell electronic configuration: 2, 8, 8.
Subshell electronic configuration: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶.
